notes.meaning: Bezalel led the work to build the ark of the covenant, a sacred chest made of durable acacia wood. It was built to the exact measurements God gave Moses, about forty-five inches long and twenty-seven inches wide and high. As the central piece of furniture in the tabernacle, it was crafted first to serve as the throne and meeting place of God among his people.

The wooden chest was covered inside and outside with pure gold, and finished with a decorative gold molding around its upper edge. Covering both the hidden inside and the visible outside showed that God desires pure devotion throughout our lives. The gold border also kept the sacred lid firmly in position.

Four gold rings were cast and attached to the four feet of the ark, and wooden poles covered in gold were slid through them. These poles allowed the priests to carry the ark safely without ever touching the sacred chest itself. Keeping the poles ready in their rings showed that God's people were always prepared to follow his leading through the wilderness.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition notes that the carrying poles were never to be removed from the rings, even later when the ark rested inside Solomon's temple, emphasizing permanent reverence for holy things.

notes.meaning: Bezalel crafted the mercy seat, a lid made of solid gold that matched the length and width of the ark. This was the place where God promised to meet with his people above the tablets of the law. Once a year on the Day of Atonement, blood was sprinkled here to turn away God's anger and wipe away the people's sins.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Thomas Aquinas taught that the mercy seat directly foreshadows Christ, who became the true place of reconciliation and the footstool of God.

notes.meaning: Two winged figures called cherubim were hammered out of the very same slab of solid gold as the mercy seat. They were not made separately and attached, but shaped together as one continuous piece. Beating such complex figures out of solid gold showed the remarkable artistic skill God gave to his workmen.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Thomas Aquinas noted that God commanded two cherubim rather than one to represent the company of heavenly angels and to keep the people from worshiping the sculpture as a single idol.

notes.meaning: The cherubim spread their wings upward over the mercy seat and looked down toward the golden cover. Their downward gaze pointed toward the place of sacrifice, picturing angels watching God's plan of mercy unfold. This posture expressed humble reverence and united service before the presence of the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Thomas Aquinas explained that the two cherubim facing each other symbolizes the mutual peace and harmony among heavenly spirits.

notes.meaning: The craftsmen built a table of acacia wood about three feet long, a foot and a half wide, and two feet high. This table held twelve loaves of bread, representing God's ongoing fellowship with the twelve tribes of Israel. It reminded the people that God continually provides for his family and invites them into his presence.

The table was covered with pure gold and bordered by a raised rim about three inches wide, with gold molding around the edges. This sturdy border prevented the bread and holy dishes from sliding off the tabletop. The rich gold overlay showed that this table served God as the true King in his palace.

Four gold rings were attached near the legs beneath the rim, and wooden poles covered in gold were passed through them. These poles enabled the priests to carry the table safely during the journey through the desert. Everything was arranged so that God's holy furniture could be moved with care and dignity.

Bezalel made all the utensils for the table out of solid gold, including plates for the bread and pitchers and bowls for drink offerings. These vessels were used in the regular worship ceremonies before the Lord. God's house was supplied with fine, durable tools for reverent service.

The lampstand was hammered out of a single piece of pure gold, with a base, a central stem, and cups shaped like blossoms with buds and petals. Unlike the ark and the table, it had no wood inside, but was solid gold throughout. Since the tabernacle had no windows, this lampstand provided the light the priests needed to do their work.

Six branches curved outward from the central shaft, three on each side, each decorated with cups shaped like almond blossoms. The almond tree was the first tree to bloom in spring, reminding the people of God's watchful care and fresh life. A decorative bud was set under each pair of branches where they joined the main stem, creating a balanced, tree-like design.

The decorative buds and branches were not made as separate pieces and welded together, but were hammered from one solid block of pure gold. This unified structure showed great skill and patience on the part of the craftsmen. It stood as a reminder of the unity and wholeness of God's people in his presence.

The workers made seven oil lamps to sit on top of the branches, along with golden tongs and trays to trim the wicks. The entire lampstand and its accessories were hammered out of one talent of pure gold, which weighed about seventy-five pounds. Its lights were tended every morning and evening so that God's sanctuary was never left in darkness.

The incense altar was built of acacia wood as a square stand about one and a half feet wide and three feet high. Its four raised corner posts, called horns, were carved as part of the frame itself. This altar stood in the Holy Place just in front of the inner curtain that separated it from the ark of the covenant.

Bezalel overlaid the top, sides, and horns of this altar with pure gold and placed a golden molding around the edge. While the outdoor altar for animal sacrifices was coated with bronze, this inner altar was covered in gold because it stood close to God's presence. The sweet incense burned here pictured the prayers of God's people rising with favor before him.

Two gold rings were attached under the molding on opposite sides, and poles of wood covered in gold were fitted through them. These poles allowed the priests to transport the altar cleanly without touching the sacred structure. Even the tools used to carry the furniture were treated with honor because they belonged to God's house.

Finally, the sacred anointing oil and fragrant incense were blended with skill according to the work of a perfumer. The special oil was used to set apart the priests and tabernacle furniture for God's holy use alone. The fragrant incense filled the sanctuary with a sweet scent, showing that worship offered God's way brings delight to him.
